solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags.note: C is the only option that paraphrases the closing thesis ('deciding what the viewer should keep'); B and D are visibly narrow/unsupported, so the item is low-discrimination.

R050-01.notes: C: the narrator moves from seeing subtitles as 'a translation with pieces missing' to 'deciding what the viewer should keep.' A: the opposite of the narrator's view, which was the view abandoned after the first year. B: dialect appears in only one anecdote; there is no claim that it is the hardest part. D: nothing is said about the supervisor's career or about how films are translated today.

flags.note: A echoes the passage directly ('filled four lines, stayed on screen for less than five seconds... unreadable'); a pure retrieval item.

R050-02.notes: A: four lines shown for under five seconds made it unreadable. B: the narrator 'translated every insult,' so none were left out. C: the dialect belonged to the original speech, not to the subtitle. D: no joke replaced the speech; the in-laws joke was for a pun in a different film moment.

flags.note: The distractors are weak (C reverses the outcome), so the item is easy for an inference question.

R050-03.notes: D: 'doesn't need to know what she said... need to know that she won' means conveying the outcome and force of the speech rather than its full content. A: this is exactly what the supervisor rejected. B: no explanation of the dialect is suggested. C: the grandmother won, so the supplier was not shown to be right.

flags.note: C is a plausible overstatement of the gestures sentence: 'say things that no subtitle could' is not 'matter more than any film's spoken dialogue.' It is ruled out cleanly but will draw some test takers.

R050-04.notes: B: every added word pulls the eyes away from faces, so readers miss gestures. A: the supervisor's single remark is in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 is not about training. C: an overstatement of the comparison, since the paragraph is about reading versus watching, not gestures against dialogue in general. D: the comedy is introduced in paragraph 2.

flags.note: B 'survives' is the closest trap through the life metaphor, but nothing suggests meaning is threatened. A fits cleanly.

R050-05.notes: 'Much of the meaning lives' in the faces means the meaning is located or found there. B: survival implies a threat, which the context does not support. C: no growth is described. D: faces do not record anything.

flags.note: Answer cue: C echoes 'made the test audience laugh at the same moment the original audience had' and 'does the same work in the scene.' D is a deliberate over-literal trap based on the in-laws example.

R050-06.notes: C: a replacement joke 'does the same work in the scene', and the success test was the laugh at the same moment. A: the passage says the joke may say 'something else.' B: length is not the criterion for jokes, and the paragraph says the answer can be 'more than the dialogue contains.' D: the in-laws joke was one instance, not a rule.

flags.note: C is a reversal trap taken from the next sentence ('At other times the answer is more...'). The distinction is clear.

R050-07.notes: A: 'Good morning' may be enough 'because the warmth is in the actor's voice.' B: the example shows that the greeting is easy to shorten, not hard to translate. C: describes the joke case, the opposite situation. D: no comparison with real life is made.

flags.note: Slight wording looseness: D's 'can tell what was cut' is a little stronger than the passage ('knows that I have made a choice'; 'can feel the difference'), but it is clearly the best answer. Not blocking.

R050-08.notes: D: the audience 'hears the actors' real voices beneath every line', so they know a choice was made. A: contradicted, since subtitles keep fewer words. B: the test audience appears only in the pun anecdote and is not presented as a requirement. C: no claim is made about novel translators being careless; the point is about the reader's lack of access to the original.

flags.note: B mirrors the final paragraph closely ('I still lose things... deciding what the viewer should keep'), which is a mild word-echo cue.

R050-09.notes: B: 'I still lose things, of course' shows acceptance, and 'deciding what the viewer should keep' redefines the job. A: the narrator denies that subtitles are 'a lesser kind of translation.' C: the narrator admits losses. D: the viewers noticing is presented as honesty, not as a source of anxiety.

flags.note: Item 10 tests the same idea as items 1 and 9 (keep versus throw away), so the set is somewhat redundant.

R050-10.notes: C: it reframes the job from throwing away to keeping. A: the original approach (keep every word) was rejected. B: no new problem is raised. D: the narrator, not the viewer, decides; 'what the viewer should keep' refers to the viewer's benefit.
